sentences.text: She went up again the next night, and the night after that.
By the fourth night she had worked out how to pick one up.
You do not catch a moth; you put your finger against the wall beside it and wait, and eventually it walks onto you, unhurried, like somebody stepping onto a bus.
The one that came onto her finger on the fourth night had a hallway painted across its wings.
A long hallway with a runner carpet, and at the end of it, a green door.
She held it under the bulb and looked at it for a long time.
The longer she looked, the more certain she became that she had walked down that hallway.
She knew what the light was like at the far end in the afternoon.
She knew the carpet had a worn patch two thirds of the way along and that you could feel it through socks.
And at exactly the same time, with exactly the same certainty, she knew that she had never been there in her life.
Her uncle came up the ladder behind her with two mugs of tea, which is a difficult thing to do and suggested practice.
He did not seem surprised by any of it.
He handed her a mug, sat down on an upturned crate that had clearly been sat on many times before, and looked at the moth on her finger.
"Green door," he said.
"That's a good one.
Somebody misses that." Ines said nothing, because she could not think of a question small enough to start with.
"People drop dreams," her uncle said.
"All the time.
The way you drop a glove out of a pocket — you don't feel it go, you just find later that you've only got the one.
Wake up too fast, somebody says your name, the alarm goes off in the wrong part of it.
And the dream falls out." He drank some tea.
"They have to go somewhere.
Everything has to go somewhere.

This house has been collecting them since before it was mine, and before it was my mother's, and I've never worked out why this house and not the one next door." "How many are there?" "I stopped counting in about nineteen ninety." Ines turned her hand slowly so the moth stayed level.

On the wall above her, a hundred pale wings held a hundred small pictures: a bicycle, a hospital corridor, a hillside with a wall across it, a wedding, a dog, a shop she was almost sure was the shop on Bridge Street but with different windows.
"Can they go back?" she said.
"Can you give one back to someone?" Her uncle looked at his tea for a while.
"That," he said, "is the difficult part."
